an2.35:1.2: “Religious donation” is _dakkhiṇa_, the offering to Vedic priests for their services; for details see [mn142:5.1]().
an2.35:1.4: A “trainee” (_sekha_) is one who has entered the ranks of the Noble Ones (_ariyapuggala_) through the realization of the four noble truths (eg. [sn48.53:3.1]()); that is to say, a stream-enterer, once-returner, or non-returner, but not an arahant, who is an “adept” beyond training (_asekha_).
an2.36:1.1: The argument of this discourse is simple: a mendicant who merely keeps the rules goes to heaven, but does not get enlightened. For that, one must meditate, developing deep immersion leading to non-return. The details, however, are not entirely clear, and taking into account the Chinese parallel at MA 21, it seems likely there is textual corruption of some sort. Compared to the Pali, the Chinese swaps the terms “internal” and “external”, and also inverts the order of exposition.
an2.36:1.2: This is the major monastery just outside Sāvatthī, a park furnished with monastic dwellings offered by Anāpiṇḍaka.
an2.36:2.1: This portion is similar in MA 21, except this person is said to have a fetter to the external instead of internal. They have restrained their conduct but not purified their mind of desire for “external” sensual pleasures. MA 21 consistently applies “internal” to the non-returner, who has no attachment to sense pleasures, but still has attachment to rebirth in realms of absorption. This seems more logical. It appears the Pali text is confused on this detail.
an2.36:3.3: This phrase occurs in one other discourse, where it describes the development of insight after tranquillity ([an4.178]()). It seems, therefore, that it could mean any of the states of immersion. | MA 21 adds here that before attaining the peaceful liberation they “train in disenchantment regarding sensual desires, abandoning sensual desires”.
an2.36:4.2: In the Pali, this practice replaces the peaceful liberation, but MA 21 says they “train in the realm of form, abandoning desire and activities” before attaining the peaceful liberation. In neither case is the distinction between the two non-returners particularly clear. It seems to me the previous non-returner emphasized serenity, whereas this one emphasizes discernment.
an2.36:5.1: Such deities are mentioned only here. _Samacitta_ (“fair-minded”) occurs at [an8.22:8.5](), where it means regarding all without prejudice.
an2.36:5.4: Apparently to inform him of the presence of the deities. At [ud4.4:7.3 ](), Sāriputta says he can’t even see a mud-goblin.
an2.36:6.9: The mental development that enabled their extraordinary abilities happened during a human life, not in heaven.
an2.36:6.11: It seems that “peaceful heart” (_santamānasa_) is meant to echo the “fair-minded” (_samacitta_) deities.
an2.36:6.14: When living in community, a meditator inspires with their calm and graceful presence. In this way, the Buddha draws together the two themes of ethical conduct and meditation.
an2.36:6.16: The response to the teaching seems extravagant given its modest content. This discourses is cited twice as the Samacittapariyāyasuttanta in the Milindapañha’s lists of significant discourses given to lay people ([mil2:61.1](), [mil6.4.2:8.2]()), and further elaborated in the commentary.
an2.37:1.2: This location is unknown and the readings uncertain. The following sutta finds Mahākaccāna in Madhurā. If the current sutta were in the same region, it would explain why Sāvatthī is said to lie in the east.
an2.38:1.3: Note _sutaṁ metaṁ_, which is similar to the opening tag _evaṁ me sutaṁ_. Like the more common phrase, it specifically refers to things you have “heard”, not events you witnessed.
an2.38:2.2: The parallel passage occurs at MN 125 and AN 2.38. MS text has kāmamajjhāvasati at AN 2.38 and kāmamajjhe vasanto at MN 125. BB has “living in the midst of sensual pleasures” at MN 125 and “dwells in sensual pleasures” at AN 2.38, with the note: “I follow Ce and Be kāmamajjhāvasati (= kāmaṁ ajjhāvasati), as against Ee kāmamajjhe vasati.” Notably, the first two terms in the sequence are reversed. the sequence in MN 125 makes better sense: it starts with where they live, what they do, what they think about, and gradually moves up to being consumed and seeking more. I take this as the correct sense and translate both passages accordingly.
an2.38:2.3: BB has “childish elder”, evidently not reading “na”.
